en.title: {{Offshore Property Map}}: who owns England and Wales, from where?
en.text: HM Land Registry publishes which overseas companies own property in England and Wales. Companies House publishes who controls those companies. Neither register carries an identifier linking the two, so the join has to be built, and built carefully, because a wrong match is a libel risk. It's the most technically serious thing I've made: around 9,700 lines of Python across 21 modules, and it refuses to publish anything a person hasn't audited.
list: Entity resolution with Splink across two government registers with no shared key
~23,000 links covering ~88% of ~91,000 affected titles, at 99.5% measured precision
Publishes the 95% lower bound next to the headline figure, not just the headline
Won't publish unless a human has audited a sample and the tooling can verify that exact version
DuckDB store, monthly change files applied by title number, FollowTheMoney export

en.title: One engine, {{33 CVs}}, four formats
en.text: My CVs are generated from Python, not edited. One definition per CV, rendered four ways: designed PDF, ATS PDF, Word and print. Two PDF renderers and two Word renderers share one engine, fonts embedded, and the PDF and Word output agree to within half a millimetre. It's a rendering engine that happens to output CVs, and it means a date or location change lands in all 33 on the next rebuild instead of drifting across thirty files.
list: 33 CVs, four formats each, plus print versions, from one shared engine
ReportLab and python-docx, one renderer per format, no duplicates (the duplicate was found and deleted)
Every build is checked for page count and banned phrases, so nothing goes stale silently

en.title: {{ISQ Agent}}, presented in person to RiverAI
en.text: A RAG agent for supplier security questionnaires, built for RiverAI's AI Engineer technical challenge and presented to them in person. It reads a blank questionnaire, PDF or XLSX, grounds every answer in the company's policy documents and past responses, drafts an answer with the citations it actually used, and scores its own confidence. The shaky ones get flagged for a human instead of being dressed up as fine.
list: Python, FastAPI, LangChain, Claude, Voyage embeddings and Pinecone
Per-question confidence scoring across four dimensions, with human-review flags
Three output formats: DOCX report, XLSX overlay on the original workbook, lossless JSON
Tokens, cost and latency logged per question, 480+ tests, CI on every push
Also ships as an installable Claude Code skill

en.title: {{The Kicker}}: a Dixon-Coles model running in the browser
en.text: Premier League predictions from a time-decayed Dixon-Coles model fitted over 33 seasons, served up as a tabloid broadsheet written by ten original AI columnists. The bit I'm proudest of is the engine. It ships as about 5 KB of fitted coefficients plus pure TypeScript, so every prediction runs client-side. No server, no tracking, and it works with no API keys at all.
list: Dixon-Coles engine, fitted and calibrated over 33 seasons, shipped as a few kilobytes of numbers
Runs entirely in the browser: no backend needed for predictions
SvelteKit front end, optional FastAPI backend for the training data and an XGBoost blend
Backtest pin gate in the test suite, so a refit that gets worse fails CI
Ten columnist personas via Claude, using an inline-token pattern for rich content inside plain prose

en.title: {{Sanctuary}} moves to native iOS
en.text: Sanctuary is a daily functioning app for neurodiverse users, built from lived experience. This spring it moved from a web reference build to native iOS: Swift, SwiftUI and SwiftData, fully on-device, built against iOS 27. You tap the orb, speak, and it sorts the ramble into tasks and a calm daily view using Apple's on-device speech and AI. Nothing leaves the phone. That isn't a feature, it's the whole design.
list: Native Swift, SwiftUI and SwiftData, in active development against iOS 27
Fully on-device: no cloud, no accounts, no tracking, works offline
600+ automated tests, plus security, privacy and accessibility audits with no critical issues open
Solo build end to end: architecture, design, code and testing

en.title: {{Version TimeTravel}}: nine versions, every one still runs
en.text: An archive of my personal site, version by version, from hand-written HTML in 2024 to a React and shadcn build today. Nine versions in two years, and every one opens and runs in the browser exactly as it shipped, inside a device frame you can flip between desktop, tablet and mobile. The gap between the first and the ninth is bigger than the gap between what I was working with in paid employment and what I use now. A CV can't make that claim. A working archive can.
list: Nine versions, two years, one person, all still running as originally shipped
Each version is the real frozen artefact, not a screenshot
Desktop, tablet and mobile viewports, keyboard navigation, deep-linkable versions
